“Before we go in,” Rashmi said, tapping the map on her phone, “where are the exits?”

“Main gate, obviously,” Sachin said.

“That's the entrance. Look. Two side doors on the left, and one behind the stage. I'll aim for the left ones if it gets rough.”

“You're being dramatic.”

“I'm being boring, and boring is good.” She held two fists up near her chest. “Arms like this if it's packed. It keeps room to breathe.”

Sachin sighed, then looked properly. Later, in the crush at the gate, a wave shoved sideways. “Don't fight it,” Rashmi called. “Go with it, toward the left door!”

They drifted with the crowd until the side door opened onto cool air.

“Okay,” Sachin gasped. “Boring is good.” Behind them Kabir laughed with relief.

I'm Anand, and I get a small knot in my stomach when a crowd thickens. At the music festival gate last month I did what Jyoti had suggested. Before we went in, we noted the two exit signs and the first-aid tent. When the crowd began to press, I kept my arms up in front of my chest. Someone behind me shoved, and my first instinct was to push back. I didn't. I let the flow carry me a few steps toward the side.

Jyoti was ahead, and she turned and pointed at the exit sign. We came out into open air. I kept thinking how easy it would have been to fight the current and get hurt.

Scout leader's note, Kumbh volunteer duty, Day 2.
At the railway station exit this evening, the crowd grew dense very fast after two trains arrived together. I watched Gautam, one of our older scouts, very closely.
Before the trains came, he had already pointed out the two side exits to the younger scouts. When the crowd thickened, he kept his arms up in front of his chest, and told Pema, who was beside him, to do the same. He didn't push back against the crowd; he moved with it, slowly, towards the side exit, holding Pema's sleeve.
When a gap opened, he guided three younger scouts out behind him. He stayed calm the whole time.
I have asked Gautam to explain his steps at tomorrow's briefing.

New Year's Eve, 2 am
Big concert at the beach tonight. Before it started, I made Vishal walk the edges with me. He rolled his eyes, but we found three exits and agreed: if we get separated, meet at the lifeguard tower.
At midnight, the fireworks went up and the crowd pushed towards the stage. Suddenly we were squashed. Vishal started pushing back, panicking. I grabbed his arm. “Arms up, like me. Don't fight it. Go with it, sideways.” We edged left, towards the second exit, step by step.
We got out onto the sand, breathing hard. Behind us, people were still pressed together.
I'm still shaky, but proud. Having a plan made me calm when it mattered.
Ishita

qa.a: At the lifeguard tower.

qa.a: Ishita feels a bit shaky but proud and calm, knowing the plan helped.

qa.a: He was probably panicking and frightened, and then relieved when Ishita gave clear instructions.

At the Shivratri mela by the Kanipura temple, before they even went in, Swati pointed out the side lane by the sweet stalls and the old well beyond it. "If we get separated, we meet at the well." Ayesha rolled her eyes but agreed.
By nine the main lane was packed tight. When the procession drums began, the crowd pressed forward. Swati felt it squeeze her ribs. She raised her arms in front of her chest, like a boxer, and told Ayesha to do the same. She didn't push back. She let the crowd carry them, stepping sideways each time it loosened, toward the sweet-stall lane. A small boy was crying beside them; Swati took his hand and kept him in front of her.
In the side lane they could breathe. They handed the boy to a policewoman at the stalls, who found his father within minutes. Ayesha, panting, said, "The well plan. I'm never laughing at you again."

qa.q: Where did Swati say they would meet if separated?
qa.a: At the well.

qa.q: How did Swati feel when the crowd squeezed her ribs?
qa.a: Swati felt the fear of it but stayed calm and focused, sticking to the plan instead of panicking.

qa.q: Which of Swati's steps kept them safe?
qa.a: Noting a side exit beforehand, keeping arms up, moving with the crowd instead of against it, and edging sideways when it loosened.

qa.q: What was it like for the small boy when Swati took his hand?
qa.a: He was frightened and crying, and holding her hand likely made him feel less lost until he was back with his father.
